notes: Original Phobos fiction, commissioned by phobosgekko on 6 October 2026; agent-authored choices open to owner revision. Vanilla evidence, literary influences and mechanical limits: docs/development/spacer-stories-vanilla-expansion.md. This pack does not change native plots, gigs, faction scores, station rules or NPCs.

spacertales-return-estimate-file.name: COMING_HOME.TXT
spacertales-return-estimate-file.text:
Freight circle: comparison copy, [place]
Compiled by [person:spacertales-dara-osei]. Private correspondence, not a posted Gig Nexus contract.

The offer was good enough to make the captain read it twice. The second reading was where it became less good. It paid for a delivery; the quoted costs described a departure.

Broker's copy: cargo collected, outward fuel, arrival, unloading.
Captain's copy: all of those; supplies during the queue; wages during the queue; another outward journey called the return; a missed collection from a relative looking after the captain's child.

The captain did not call the broker a liar. They asked who would pay for the part of the job beyond the final line. The broker answered that the reward was unusually generous. The captain agreed. It still had to cover the journey.

A second offer arrived with a later date. The captain declined that one too: more time had not repaired the costs. A third let the captain quote a route they were already planning. That was the one they took.

The circle has kept this as an example of a successful negotiation. The broker calls it a lost afternoon. Both statements are true.

No fuel prices, route times or arrival guarantees can be inferred from this historical case. Your 300-credit reading fee is separate from the delivery. Its copying account is now closed.

spacertales-working-label-file.name: WORKING_NAMES.TXT
spacertales-working-label-file.text:
Maintenance label correspondence, [place]
Copy held by [person:spacertales-noor-iman]. The original pump remains offscreen; no title or safety finding is made here.

There were three sale cards and one label. The cards changed with the owners. The label changed with the work.

A date had a second date beside it because the replacement seal had failed early. A warning was squeezed around an older signature because nobody wanted to cover the signature. One name was crossed out and rewritten larger: the worker had taught a replacement who wanted the name legible.

The newest seller thought the crossing-out might worry a customer. The former maintainer thought cutting it away ought to worry a customer. The pump was ordinary. It did not hide a secret cargo or a message from a vanished captain. It had simply been worth enough effort for people to write things down.

In a separate account there were wages still disputed from the first refit. The label did not settle them, and the clerk would not let its preservation be described as settlement. The old crew can still have a claim even when a new owner has clean sale papers.

The seller kept the current sale card and enclosed a copy of the label. The former maintainer said that would do, for now.

Reader's comparison used a Bingham-12 EVA battery only as an example of a short equipment name. Its condition, charge, history and ownership were not tested.

spacertales-away-address-file.name: WHILE_AWAY.TXT
spacertales-away-address-file.text:
Berth neighbours: revised contact sheet, [place]
Filed by [person:spacertales-laleh-ade]. A voluntary agreement among the neighbours named in the private original.

A berth number tells you where a vessel was. It is less useful when the vessel has gone somewhere else. The first sheet gave a returning neighbour an old number and a note saying gone away. Their letters had spent the whole run in the correct station and the wrong drawer.

The new sheet has three lines: last berth; person willing to receive messages; information that person has agreed to pass on. The agreement can be withdrawn. A blank line is allowed. Nobody has to invent a family to satisfy a form.

We deleted responsible party. It had sounded tidy. Then someone asked whether holding a letter meant taking over a loan. We could not agree that it meant anything of the sort, so we stopped writing it.

The neighbour's oldest recovered letter contained a request to bring tea. The request had arrived too late. Tea arrived anyway.

The association did not obtain new residency rights, pay a ship's debts or persuade a port to stop charging for a berth. It now knows where to put a letter, and it has written down the limits of what the person holding it has offered. That was the work we could do.

Separate from this case, a food rack or a reliable galley can make visits easier to host. It cannot settle a neighbour's legal address.

spacertales-petition-age-file.name: FIRST_DATE.TXT
spacertales-petition-age-file.text:
Old-ring petition: comparison copy, [place]
Prepared by [person:spacertales-ren-wu]. Private housing correspondence; no CCRE policy or tenancy right is created.

The first sheet asked for repairs. The second sheet asked why the repairs had not begun. The third sheet was an office copy of the second. By the time it reached the contractor, the date on the third sheet had become the date of the complaint.

It was possible to make every page look cleaner while making the wait disappear. Nobody needed to forge a signature. They only needed to stop carrying the first page forward.

The latch was not the largest fault. It was the one beside the berth of a worker who slept between shifts. A former neighbour had drawn it with a thick arrow and the words this one. Their letter, received later, said they still sometimes woke at home thinking they had heard it.

We copied the original date onto the clean cover and attached all three sheets. The contractor acknowledged the bundle. This does not mean the work has been authorised, scheduled or completed.

The tenant beside the latch wrote: Please leave that sentence in. Last time the copy sounded as if we had won something.

The drawing comparison could be read by a reader with civil engineering or with the former colleague's annotation. Neither route made a physical repair.

spacertales-two-descriptions-file.name: ONE_BOX.TXT
spacertales-two-descriptions-file.text:
Freight description comparison, [place]
Prepared by [person:spacertales-matti-sorell]. This copy is not a customs decision.

The broker described a used galley heater, a serviceable pan, two replacement fittings and a box of hand tools. The sender described the same things as household effects.

The heater had been bought after a crew began eating in different watches. The pan was the one large enough to keep a portion aside. The tools belonged to a household in which fixing other people's equipment paid for supper.

The broker said a description needed to be clear enough for a sale. The sender agreed, then asked why a sale needed to make the earlier household invisible.

Their first exchange was sharp. The second was practical: retain the item list, append the sender's letter, do not describe the letter as proof of ownership. Neither party agreed about the value. They agreed about what they would let the next reader see.

A translation note: household effects is the sender's description; used equipment is the broker's. The comparison offers neither a tariff classification nor a legal conclusion.

The letter accompanying the pan reads: There are people who would rather have this delivered late than sold promptly. Please ask before deciding for us.

spacertales-yard-supper-file.name: AFTER_LAUNCH.TXT
spacertales-yard-supper-file.text:
Family archive: launch evening, [place]
Filed by [person:spacertales-june-havel]. One yard account, not a description of every Titan employer.

The service craft was finished. Its launch photograph showed the customer, a supervisor and the people free to attend. The people who covered the launch watch were still aboard.

At home, a family had laid out supper for six. The youngest person asked whether the ship could wait. Somebody explained why it could not. Nobody had a good explanation for why the family had not been told earlier that the worker could not be spared.

The worker returned with a folded launch programme and ate from a covered pan. The sick colleague sent an apology. The family wrote back that the colleague had not arranged the photograph or the staffing.

A supervisor offered a name in the bulletin. The family accepted the name and asked, separately, for a day off that would stay a day off. Those were two requests; the reply had answered only one.

The next invitation read: A meal after the last watch. Portions kept for anyone covering it.

This is not a victory over the yard. The copied invitation remains a proposal between these correspondents. It is a record of people finding a smaller promise they might actually keep.

spacertales-unfinished-works-file.name: NEXT_SHIFT.TXT
spacertales-unfinished-works-file.text:
Unfinished works archive, [place]
Comparison by [person:spacertales-pema-das]. An incomplete contractor account; identifying site details are withheld.

The closing invoice gives every account an end. The works list does not. It has a door still to be hung, an exposed run to be covered and a meal-room table that somebody wanted moved before the next shift.

The list was copied in two hands. The second hand preserved the words next shift without adding a date. A former contractor recognised the sequence and said the small jobs were the ones workers expected to finish after the larger installation. They were not signs of an original plan to leave the place empty.

The meal order was for more people than the final payroll named. One worker said the extra meals had been for subcontractors. Another remembered a visitor. The archive records both recollections. It cannot resolve them from the surviving sheet.

A visitor to the archive wanted a mysterious explanation for the abandoned table. The former contractor said somebody had eaten at it and expected to eat there again. That was mysterious enough to the visitor.

This account supplies no access coordinates, evidence about the Hotel Mare Imbrium incidents or explanation of any supernatural phenomenon. The workers' departure is not dated beyond the source's own incomplete record. The archive has kept an interrupted expectation, not discovered the cause of Luna's decline.

spacertales-shift-view-file.name: THE_VIEW.TXT
spacertales-shift-view-file.text:
Family correspondence: maintenance residency, [place]
Copy held by [person:spacertales-wen-park]. A private family account; the worker's name is withheld in this copy.

My brother writes that the water is beautiful. He writes that the work is skilled. He writes that people would give anything to live where he lives. Then he asks whether we can put off coming again.

The terms explain the work that permits him to stay. The letters explain why leaving would mean losing things he spent years getting. When we tell him that sounds difficult, he reminds us how many people still want his place. He is right about them. That does not answer what we asked.

On one visit, he had arranged to show us a public view of the lake. Another worker needed their watch covered. We saw the view without him. He later sent a photograph from almost the same place, taken between tasks.

We wrote: You do not owe us gratitude on behalf of the colony. We would like a meal with you.

He answered that meals were easier to arrange than visits. Then the message stopped for three days. It resumed with an apology and a picture of the water.

The next letter will be written on a day off. He does not say when. We have kept a place at the table in our own calendar without giving the place a date.

This copy establishes no universal visa contract, salary, escape route or change to colonial policy. The worker's terms remain their own. The family's account remains a reason to read past the view.

spacertales-extra-voice-file.name: TEA_IS_READY.TXT
spacertales-extra-voice-file.text:
Night service account, [place]
Compiled by [person:spacertales-simone-kerr]. A copied recollection and timing notes, not research data.

The hired project had closed. The team had left its bench list; the service shift had its own list. Clean the shared room. Count the returned tools. Find who had taken the mug.

Two people were on the shift. The voice in their service recording says that the tea is ready. They both remember hearing it. One remembers the sound from the doorway. The other remembers it from the room speaker. Neither can name a visitor.

A former technician suggests a replay of an earlier remark. The notes contain a small timing discrepancy that could fit that explanation. They also contain the same discrepancy in a line both staff agree was spoken on the shift. The technician has written possible beside replay, and underlined the word.

The cleaner says there was tea, because they made it. They arrived after the disputed remark. They are less interested in identifying the voice than in being identified as the person who supplied the pot, washed it and returned the tools the researchers left.

We have included their name in the private original and their work in this public copy. The timing notes remain inconclusive. No project team has contributed research material to this copy. The service shift is preserving an uncertain experience, not reporting a discovery.

Final staff note: Please stop calling it the haunted tea room. We still have to use it.

Second staff note: I did not call it that until you asked me to stop.

spacertales-missing-invoice-file.name: STILL_WAITING.TXT
spacertales-missing-invoice-file.text:
Freight letters after a loss, [place]
Edited by [person:spacertales-ines-duarte]. Names and route details withheld. No confirmed location of the missing vessel is available.

The first bill was for the shipment. The second was for keeping the shipment in an account while enquiries continued. The third treated it as a loss. The bills could be reconciled more easily than the letters.

An office described the consignment as closed. A family member wrote back: Is that a word for the case, or for my sister?

The office apologised for the wording and repeated that it could provide no confirmed news of the crew. The reply made the distinction clearer. It did not make the news better.

Some correspondents blamed piracy. Others thought a transfer failure more likely. None supplied evidence sufficient to choose between them. This copy preserves those as suggestions, not a finding about the shipment or an account of every Venusian loss.

The family eventually agreed that the cargo claim could close. It asked, separately, to leave a return contact on file. The office had been using one sheet for both. It now uses two for this case.

On the second sheet, under what information is wanted, the family wrote: Anything confirmed. Even if it is late.

The card concludes this correspondence. It does not conclude the family's wait.

spacertales-family-envelope-file.name: BOTH_LETTERS.TXT
spacertales-family-envelope-file.text:
Family correspondence copy, [place]
Held by [person:spacertales-tomas-bell]. Private family letters, retained together at the writers' request.

Letter one says the restrictions have a political purpose. It asks the recipient to distinguish the purpose from the people enforcing it badly. It then asks whether the youngest cousin has been eating properly.

Letter two says it is difficult to distinguish a purpose from an empty shelf. It answers that the cousin is eating, then asks whether the writer of letter one has managed another visit to their father.

The return address on letter one is corrected in the margin of letter two. The recipe enclosed with letter two is corrected in the margin of letter one. Both writers insist their own correction is necessary.

Neither accepts the other's political argument. Neither asks for their words to be copied without the other's answer. They agree that this would make the exchange look more settled, and less truthful.

The custodian does not endorse either argument. This copy is family correspondence. It contains no route or cargo permission through the blockade.

Last line of letter two: You can be wrong and still be expected at supper. Write before you travel.

Last line of letter one: I would prefer not to be wrong. I will write.

spacertales-meal-book-file.name: MEAL_WITH_SHIFT.TXT
spacertales-meal-book-file.text:
Three dockside books, [place]
Compared by [person:spacertales-rafe-kito]. A private dispute; the copied agreement concerns these parties only.

The payer's book had a loan. The helper's book had unpaid work. The cook's book had the food they had bought for a person who covered the crowded evening.

At first the payer said the loan could be forgiven. The helper said that forgiving it would leave the loan in the story. They had not borrowed a meal. They had worked a shift.

The cook had another objection: the payer had not bought the portion. That was in the third book, beside an ordinary purchase of food for the room. It was not a donation to the payer and could not be charged again to the helper.

The payer offered an allowance. The helper asked whether an allowance would disappear next time somebody wanted the accounts balanced.

The final wording was meal with shift. The charge was crossed out in the original. The copied books retain the crossed-out line because the cook did not want the disagreement to disappear along with the money.

Nobody in this copy is asking a visiting captain to settle the account. The corrected entry concerns the helper's meal; it attaches no charge to the reader.

The cook still buys the occasional extra portion. They now write who it is for before the payer can think of another name for it.

spacertales-waiting-letter-file.name: NO_ARRIVAL_DATE.TXT
spacertales-waiting-letter-file.text:
Family letter copy, [place]
Entrusted through [person:spacertales-dara-osei] for [person:spacertales-june-havel] at the shipyards on Titan. No expiry; no exclusive or uniquely tracked cargo.

I am sending this with a captain who may eventually go your way. I have been told not to write urgent unless I mean it. I do not mean it.

Is the chair still there? The one that caught the sleeve of my good jacket. I accused whoever repaired it of designing a trap for people with somewhere better to go. It was a poor joke, and I remember you going quiet.

It has taken me much longer to send an apology than it would have taken to fix the sleeve. You do not need to reply quickly to make up the difference.

I remember the meal in that room, the covered pan for the late watch, and somebody checking whether the person still aboard the service craft had eaten. I am no longer certain who did which thing. I am certain I was treated better than I had earned.

If the chair has gone, I would still like to know how you are.

Correspondence terms: receipt at the Titan shipyard station pays the visiting captain 600 credits once; no dedicated voyage, departure schedule or return journey is requested. The text is already entrusted; the receiving check does not require this particular data card to be carried.

spacertales-waiting-reply-file.name: THE_CHAIR_STAYS.TXT
spacertales-waiting-reply-file.text:
Family reply, [place]
Copied by [person:spacertales-june-havel]. Received through the unhurried correspondence.

The chair is still here. Somebody has repaired it again. You would need to work much harder to catch a sleeve on it now.

I remember the joke. I went quiet because I had been the one who repaired the chair, and because I was tired. Neither fact was obvious. The joke was ordinary. So was being hurt by it for a moment.

You need not explain a whole journey to explain that evening. You came for a meal. People made room. You said something you regretted and have now said so.

The covered pan was my aunt's doing. The check on the late watch was a neighbour's. The service craft had no trouble leaving the next day. The people in the room had the ordinary trouble of getting through another shift.

Come when you can. Write when you cannot. There will be a chair.

Archive note: This exchange sits beside the launch-evening account because they describe different occasions in the same family room. It does not prove the same workers covered both launches. The visiting captain's 600-credit receipt closes their part of the correspondence; no return delivery is required.

spacertales-article-earth-address.label: Addresses after Earth
spacertales-article-earth-address.title: The address that cannot receive a letter
spacertales-article-earth-address.body:
Earth's orbital ablation cascade left the System cut off from a ravaged homeworld. An old address can remain in a family's papers long after it has stopped being a practical destination.

For people making their lives offworld, that address may describe a remembered home, a place known only through somebody else's stories, or a line they keep copying because dropping it would feel like losing more than a location. Families need not agree about which memory belongs in the next letter.

An offworld return address is often less permanent: a berth, a workplace, a relative or somebody willing to hold messages. A working ship adds another difficulty. The people living aboard may be reachable through several places without belonging comfortably to any of them.

Remembering Earth is not the same as knowing what now happens there. A family account can preserve a connection without settling the condition of the world behind it.

spacertales-article-shipping-stop.label: A stop becomes a place
spacertales-article-shipping-stop.title: Life around a shipping stop
spacertales-article-shipping-stop.body:
K-Leg began as an Ayotimiwa shipping stop in 2032. Fuel, supplies, a dormitory and a bar belonged to the practical business of keeping vessels moving. Only part of that first settlement survived into the station known today.

A stop also collects people whose next departure becomes less certain: a worker waiting for wages, a crew member staying with a friend, a contractor who finds another contract before leaving. Places meant to serve a journey can acquire lives of their own.

Port work and home life then share corridors. The noise that means somebody else has a job may mean somebody cannot sleep. A useful contact might be a broker, a neighbour or the person who remembers where a letter was put.

Station residents need not experience a port as captains do. For one person it is a place to get supplied and depart. For another, departure is what the neighbours keep doing around their home.

spacertales-article-salvage-household.label: Salvage and a household
spacertales-article-salvage-household.title: What a used part carries with it
spacertales-article-salvage-household.body:
A salvage economy turns parts of one vessel into supplies for another. The sale concerns the object, its condition and the price somebody will pay. The working history can be less tidy.

A part may have been maintained by a crew who never owned it, bought with borrowed money, or repaired during a watch that nobody remembered to count. A short sale name cannot hold all of that. Crews sometimes keep old labels and notes for practical warnings; they also keep them because the previous ship was somebody's home.

A remembered history is not a safety test or proof of ownership. Nor does a clean sale card necessarily answer a former worker's question about wages. Those questions can coexist without a convenient verdict.

A useful account distinguishes the object being sold from the claims people attach to it. A kind account leaves room for the people as well.

spacertales-article-freight-deadlines.label: Freight and time
spacertales-article-freight-deadlines.title: The journey behind the reward
spacertales-article-freight-deadlines.body:
A freight offer combines money, a destination and a clock. A captain has to compare those with the ship they actually have and the work that follows arrival.

The outward leg is not the whole job. Waiting consumes supplies and crew time; unloading does not put the vessel back where its next work begins. A fee can be generous and still leave the captain carrying costs the offer has not acknowledged.

Crews have reasons to prefer work already along their route, local errands while in port, or letters that can travel whenever the ship does. An urgent consignment has reasons to pay for urgency. Neither makes an impossible promise easier to keep.

An estimate is a comparison, not a guarantee. The useful question is whether the captain can complete the work with a ship and crew still ready for life afterwards. A reward alone cannot answer it.

spacertales-article-ceres-neighbours.label: Neighbours on Ceres
spacertales-article-ceres-neighbours.title: A repair request has a history
spacertales-article-ceres-neighbours.body:
Ceres holds port trade, political institutions and places where ordinary people live. The goods passing through a terminal belong to the same world as the neighbours waiting for somebody to repair a fault beside their berth.

A small fault can have a large place in a person's day. A latch rattles through a sleep period. A cupboard that does not close becomes the thing everybody learns to walk around. A report can rank these below larger work without making them stop affecting the people beside them.

Residents keep copies because each fresh description risks losing the wait behind it. The first date, a sketch and a former neighbour's signature may matter more than the neatness of the latest cover.

An acknowledged petition is not a completed repair. Local accounts often preserve that distinction more carefully than a success notice does. They belong to the history of habitation as much as the large plans for the place.

spacertales-article-lunar-expectation.label: Unfinished lunar life
spacertales-article-lunar-expectation.title: What workers expected to finish
spacertales-article-lunar-expectation.body:
Much of Luna's infrastructure was left incomplete as business interests moved toward Mars and the Belt. Abandoned working spaces preserve things that were once ordinary: unfinished installations, equipment, meals and interrupted recreation.

To a later visitor, a room can look as though it was always meant to be empty. A works list may tell another story. Small jobs marked for a later shift suggest people who expected to return, finish the installation and sit down together again.

A closing account can describe the end of a contractor's involvement without describing the state of every room. The space and the paperwork preserve different kinds of ending.

Luna also has disturbing histories that an ordinary work record cannot explain. Unfinished wiring, a preserved meal and an uncertain recollection should not be made into proof of a larger mystery merely because they survived in an unsettling place.

spacertales-article-visas-and-hours.label: Maintenance and residency
spacertales-article-visas-and-hours.title: Permission to stay, time to live
spacertales-article-visas-and-hours.body:
Hangzhou Orbital's desirable living conditions create intense pressure around access and residency. Maintenance work visas were intended to admit people needed to maintain the colony; the setting also records their use in indentured servitude.

A worker can have permission to live in a place and still have little freedom to enjoy it. The work that keeps the address may occupy the time a family visit would need. Leaving may cost the worker things they have spent years obtaining.

This pressure reaches a family through ordinary arrangements: postponed visits, watches exchanged, a meal planned around a day off that later moves. A beautiful view can be sincerely loved and still appear in a letter explaining another absence.

The colony's desirability does not make every employment term identical. Private accounts are useful precisely because they show what a particular worker can do, what they cannot afford to do, and what other people see from outside.

spacertales-article-deimos-service.label: Between research shifts
spacertales-article-deimos-service.title: The work between the projects
spacertales-article-deimos-service.body:
Voltaire's facilities on Deimos combine research, rented laboratory space, high-tech manufacturing and a university supported by Brave New World. The visible work of a project depends on less visible work that continues when a team leaves.

Supplies must be counted. Shared rooms need cleaning. Tools have to be found and returned. A service worker's account may span several projects whose summaries describe themselves as separate beginnings and endings.

People who work those hours know a facility through repeated small tasks: a door that sticks, a mug everyone claims, a delivery that regularly arrives between watches. Their familiarity can be useful without granting them access to a project's results or an explanation of every unusual experience.

A research history and a service history answer different questions. Keeping them beside each other gives the people maintaining the place a life beyond being the last line of somebody else's report.

spacertales-article-venus-loss.label: Freight after a loss
spacertales-article-venus-loss.title: Accounts and people who wait
spacertales-article-venus-loss.body:
Venusian trade faces piracy around atmospheric transfers and local shipments. A lost or delayed consignment affects more than the accounts of the people paying for it.

A freight office may need a date for delay, a date for loss and a date for closing a claim. Families waiting for crew may have no reason to accept any of those as the end of their questions. The same word can be useful in a cargo account and painful when applied to a person.

Unconfirmed reports can carry practical hope and attract people with less helpful interests. A responsible copy can preserve a return contact while withholding details that would turn a family's wait into a rumour about valuable cargo.

An insurer, a carrier and a relative can agree on the contents of a file while asking different things of it. Closing one account does not supply an answer for every person attached to the journey.

spacertales-article-europa-mail.label: Families across restrictions
spacertales-article-europa-mail.title: The family remains in the letter
spacertales-article-europa-mail.body:
The Confederacy's blockade at Porto Nuevo restricts offworld trade with Atlantis after the Ganymede Coup. Political purpose, enforcement and the cost to ordinary households need not look the same from each side.

Relatives can disagree about that politics while continuing to ask after one another. A letter may argue about a restriction, correct a return address, ask whether somebody is eating and preserve a recipe on the same page. These are not interruptions of the political story; they are some of the lives the story concerns.

Preserving both letters can keep a disagreement visible without treating it as a broken relationship. The family may refuse to give a later reader the comfort of a single settled account.

Such correspondence creates no route through the blockade and grants no permission to carry cargo. Its importance may be that, despite disagreement and distance, the writers still expect another letter.

spacertales-article-titan-calendar.label: People around a launch
spacertales-article-titan-calendar.title: The shipyard has more than one calendar
spacertales-article-titan-calendar.body:
Titan is a centre of advanced ships, habitats and military-industrial activity. Around those capabilities are workers and households organising ordinary lives.

A launch schedule, a shift roster and a family calendar can describe the same evening differently. A craft leaves on time; someone stays aboard to cover a watch; a meal ashore is put away. The successful departure does not make the missed meal imaginary.

A name in a bulletin may be welcome and still fail to answer a request for time off. A family can admire the ship while wishing the worker had been free to sit beside them.

Accounts of people around a launch add another measure of its cost. They need not deny the technical achievement to ask whose time made it possible, and who had enough left to enjoy the celebration.

spacertales-article-help-and-wages.label: Help, wages and debt
spacertales-article-help-and-wages.title: The name given to a payment
spacertales-article-help-and-wages.body:
An informal agreement can leave several accounts of the same exchange. One person remembers help, another remembers wages, and a third is handed a debt.

A meal offered during work may be described later as a favour. The person who bought it may be absent from the account altogether. Changing the description can change who seems generous and who seems obliged, even when no goods change hands again.

Crews and dockside workers keep private books because comparing them can reveal that disagreement. A corrected entry can settle a particular charge without settling every relationship around it. Keeping the old wording crossed out preserves why the correction mattered.

Informal kindness remains valuable. Naming what was actually offered helps keep kindness from being turned into an obligation nobody agreed to accept.
